newsitem.title: USA: U.S. natgas, western power prices move in tandem.
newsitem.headline: U.S. natgas, western power prices move in tandem.

text.p: Natural gas prices have been a key driver in the western U.S. power market this winter despite the fact that gas accounts for less than 10 percent of the region's electricity generation.
"Last year the power market was completely disengaged from gas on the West Coast. That obviously hasn't happened this year," said Toby Voge, power contracts supervisor at Tucson Electric Power.
Instead, the markets have moved in lock-step over the past couple of months with natgas prices often cited as the single most important indicator of daily power price direction.
Sources cited near-average hydropower conditions, lower gas storage volumes, more flexible gas pipeline operations and increased use of "must run" gas-fired power plants as factors behind the shift.

They noted natural gas is typically the fuel-on-margin for western power production during heavy demand periods, except in years - like the October 1995-September 1996 water year - with much higher than normal hydroelectric output.
"Right now, the short-term market is for power to displace gas plants," explained Bobby Campo, senior marketer at Portland General Electric Co's California office.
He explained that utilities will buy higher-priced spot power during peak demand hours as long as overall costs are low enough to justify idling more expensive gas-fired plants.
December San Juan gas surged this week to about $4.00 per million British thermal units, more than three times what it was a year ago.
In addition, the differential between San Juan and Henry Hub natgas recently has narrowed to almost even, compared with more than a $1.00 Hub premium at this time last year.

Gas prices typically rise in winter - when most of the nation sees higher heating demand. But western gas prices were relatively isolated from this seasonal volatility in recent years, due in large part to increased pipeline capacity for shipments from Canada.
According to the California Energy Commission, Canadian supplies accounted for 29 percent of statewide gas usage last year, up from 18 percent in 1991.
Market sources said many players, expecting the supply glut to continue this year, shaved inventories.
"I think a lot of people decided to reduce storage. There has been a little bit of panic mixed in," now that prices are rising, said another trade source.
More flexibility with previously captive pipeline volumes from Texas into the Southwest has also helped bring western prices more in line with the rest of the U.S., sources said.
Bill Cordes, president of Enron Corp's Transwestern Pipeline Co, said work was completed this summer on the line which allows San Juan gas to flow east as well as west.
"Producers who used to be stuck going to California now have more choices," Cordes said.
El Paso Energy, which operates a natural gas pipeline running from Texas to the California border, has also increased the flexibility of its operations.
"At times we have 70 to 100 million cubic feet per day moving east, but it depends on the market," an El Paso engineer said.

In addition, some industry sources say constraints on high-voltage interstate transmission lines - put in place as a precaution after two major regional power outages this summer - mean more higher-cost gas plants remain on-line in the West.
Meanwhile, market analysts expect some de-coupling of the two markets by spring, when above-normal snowpack in the Pacific Northwest and California is seen leading to healthy hydropower generation.
--D Beasley, Los Angeles bureau + 1 213 955 6761
